subtopic_detail: Smoking cessation pharmacotherapy in a patient with prior seizure
stem:
You are the general practice registrar in a bulk billing clinic. A 44 year old man attends to discuss quitting smoking. He smokes 25 cigarettes daily and has smoked for 25 years with a Fagerstrom score of 7. He has attempted quitting twice with nicotine gum alone and relapsed within a month. He has type 2 diabetes on metformin, a body mass index of 32, and had one alcohol withdrawal seizure 10 years ago after which he became abstinent from alcohol.

His medications are metformin 1 g twice daily and atorvastatin 20 mg at night. He has no history of psychiatric illness, no suicidal thoughts and no cardiovascular disease. Vital signs are pulse 78, blood pressure 128/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius. Bloods 2 weeks ago showed HbA1c 6.7 percent (under 5.7 percent), eGFR 82 mL/min/1.73m2 (over 60), ALT 32 U/L (5-45).

He is highly motivated to quit and has agreed a quit date in 2 weeks.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 128/82 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.History: Smoking 25/day for 25 years, Fagerstrom 7, previously failed nicotine gum alone, type 2 diabetes, one prior alcohol withdrawal seizure, BMI 32

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate first line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Bupropion 150 mg orally daily for 3 days then 150 mg twice daily for 12 weeks under close observation
options.rationale: Bupropion lowers seizure threshold and is contraindicated with any history of seizure disorder including alcohol withdrawal seizure; varenicline is safer here (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Varenicline 0.5 mg orally daily for 3 days, then 0.5 mg twice daily for 4 days, then 1 mg twice daily for 12 weeks
options.rationale: Varenicline is the most effective single agent for smoking cessation and preferred over bupropion here because bupropion lowers seizure threshold and he has a prior withdrawal seizure; RACGP endorses varenicline in patients without recent cardiovascular event or serious mental illness (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation; Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular).

options.text: Nicotine patch 21 mg daily alone for 12 weeks with no oral pharmacotherapy under close observation
options.rationale: Monotherapy nicotine replacement has already failed him; combination NRT (patch plus rapid rescue) or varenicline is more effective for heavy dependence (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation).

options.text: Nortriptyline 25 mg orally at night titrated to 75 to 100 mg over 4 weeks under close observation
options.rationale: Nortriptyline is second line for smoking cessation and carries anticholinergic and cardiotoxic risks; it is not preferred where varenicline is safe and effective (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation).

options.text: Clonidine 25 micrograms twice daily titrated to 75 micrograms twice daily under close observation
options.rationale: Clonidine is a third line agent with adverse effect burden (sedation, hypotension, rebound hypertension); it is not appropriate as first choice (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation).

explanation.summary: Smoking cessation pharmacotherapy in Australia offers three first line options: combination NRT (long acting patch plus rapid acting gum or lozenge), varenicline, or bupropion. Varenicline (alpha4 beta2 partial nicotinic agonist) has the highest single agent efficacy but requires review of cardiovascular history and any serious psychiatric illness. Bupropion (noradrenergic and dopaminergic reuptake inhibitor) is effective but contraindicated with seizure disorder, eating disorder, or MAOI use. Combination NRT is the recommended NRT approach for moderate to heavy dependence, and behavioural support doubles quit rates alongside pharmacotherapy.
key_points: First line: combination NRT, varenicline, or bupropion
Bupropion contraindicated in seizure disorder or eating disorder
Varenicline is the most effective single agent
Combination NRT for Fagerstrom over 5
Behavioural support doubles quit rate
explanation.pearls: The EAGLES trial (2016) showed varenicline is safe in stable psychiatric illness with no significant increase in neuropsychiatric adverse events compared with placebo, patch, or bupropion; the FDA black box warning was removed.

subtopic_detail: Valproate in a woman of reproductive age with bipolar
stem:
You are the community psychiatry registrar. A 28 year old woman with bipolar I disorder has been maintained for 2 years on sodium valproate 1200 mg daily with good mood stabilisation after two failed lithium trials (rash, nausea intolerance). She uses barrier contraception intermittently, has an irregular menstrual cycle, and reports her partner and she are considering starting a family in the next year.

Her last valproate level 4 weeks ago was 520 micromol/L (350-700). She has no current mood symptoms, is not suicidal, and works full time as a school teacher. She has no medical conditions and does not smoke. She has heard from a friend that valproate is unsafe in pregnancy and asks whether she should stop it now.

Her weight is 74 kg, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, and she is up to date with cervical screening.

data_table.Medication history: Sodium valproate 1200 mg daily for 2 years, prior lithium trials failed (rash, nausea)
data_table.Reproductive: Age 28, uses barrier contraception intermittently, irregular cycle, considering pregnancy in next year
data_table.Investigations: Valproate level 520 micromol/L (350-700) four weeks ago; weight 74 kg; BP 118/74 mmHg

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate management step?

options.text: Continue valproate at current dose and add folic acid 500 micrograms daily
options.rationale: Continuing valproate exposes any future pregnancy to a 10 percent major malformation risk and dose dependent neurodevelopmental impairment; folic acid does not mitigate this risk (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Bipolar Disorder; TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Program).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Bipolar Disorder

options.text: Continue valproate and start a 3 month combined oral contraceptive pill without switching
options.rationale: Effective contraception is necessary during valproate use but the plan is to switch away from valproate before conception; contraception alone does not address the desired pregnancy timeline (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Program).

options.text: Stop valproate abruptly today with no substitute pharmacotherapy or contraception adjustment
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation of a mood stabiliser in bipolar I risks rapid relapse into mania or depression; a planned taper with alternative mood stabiliser and effective contraception is required (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Bipolar Disorder).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Bipolar Disorder

options.text: Reduce valproate to 600 mg daily to minimise dose dependent teratogenicity
options.rationale: There is no safe dose of valproate in pregnancy; even under 500 mg/day the malformation risk exceeds background and neurodevelopmental risk is present; the AU program is switch, not reduce (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Program).

options.text: Cross taper valproate to lamotrigine and arrange effective contraception until switch complete
options.rationale: AU TGA and RANZCP guidance are that valproate should not be prescribed to women of reproductive potential unless other options have failed and effective contraception is in place; here lamotrigine is a first line alternative and switch with effective contraception is required (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Bipolar Disorder; TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Program).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Bipolar Disorder

explanation.summary: Valproate is the most teratogenic anti-seizure medication in current AU use: 10 percent major congenital malformation rate (neural tube, cardiac, orofacial, hypospadias), and up to 30 to 40 percent risk of neurodevelopmental impairment including autism and lower IQ. The TGA restricts valproate in women and girls of reproductive potential to those in whom other options have failed AND with effective contraception (pregnancy prevention program). Lamotrigine, lithium (with foetal cardiac surveillance), and second generation antipsychotics (olanzapine, quetiapine) are safer bipolar mood stabilisers in reproductive age women. Switching is planned with pharmacist input to avoid relapse.
key_points: Valproate causes 10 percent major malformation and 30-40 percent NDD risk
Not for reproductive age women unless other options have failed
Effective contraception required during use
Lamotrigine, lithium, quetiapine are safer bipolar options
Switch is planned, not abrupt
explanation.pearls: Lamotrigine cross-titration to valproate requires very slow titration (starting 25 mg every other day) because valproate inhibits lamotrigine metabolism, doubling risk of severe rash including Stevens Johnson syndrome.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Bipolar Disorder

subtopic_detail: Adult sepsis hour-1 bundle in a patient with urinary source
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar. A 72 year old woman is brought in by ambulance with 8 hours of fever, rigors, and confusion. Her daughter reports she has become unable to stand and has been passing dark strong smelling urine for 24 hours. Her background includes type 2 diabetes, hypertension and osteoarthritis. Her medications are metformin, perindopril and paracetamol.

On arrival she is drowsy but rousable to voice. Vital signs are pulse 128, blood pressure 82/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 26, SpO2 94 percent on 6 L/min oxygen by simple face mask, temperature 38.9 degrees Celsius. Bedside investigations: capillary glucose 12.4 mmol/L (3.5-7.7), lactate 4.6 mmol/L (under 2), venous pH 7.28 (7.35-7.45), bicarbonate 16 mmol/L (22-32), sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), creatinine 172 micromol/L (45-90).

Her chest is clear on auscultation and her abdomen is soft with mild suprapubic tenderness. She is on continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring and 20 gauge intravenous access is established in each antecubital fossa.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128, BP 82/48 mmHg, RR 26, SpO2 94% on 6 L/min O2, temperature 38.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, clear chest, soft abdomen with suprapubic tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 12.4 mmol/L (3.5-7.7), lactate 4.6 mmol/L (<2), venous pH 7.28 (7.35-7.45), bicarbonate 16 mmol/L (22-32), Na 138 mmol/L (135-145), K 4.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), creatinine 172 micromol/L (45-90)

lead_in: In addition to blood and urine cultures, oxygen, IV fluids and empirical antibiotics, what is the single most appropriate hour-1 addition to her management?

options.text: Broad spectrum empirical antifungal fluconazole 800 mg intravenous added to antibiotics
options.rationale: Empirical antifungal is not part of the initial hour-1 bundle in most sepsis and is added only for identified risk factors such as immunosuppression or prolonged broad spectrum antibiotic exposure (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Hydrocortisone 200 mg intravenous over 24 hours by continuous infusion with senior clinical review
options.rationale: Steroids are added only for shock refractory to fluid and vasopressor; giving before vasopressor is initiated is out of order (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign).

options.text: Repeat 30 mL/kg intravenous crystalloid bolus over a further 30 minutes irrespective of clinical response
options.rationale: Fluid resuscitation is 30 mL/kg over the first 3 hours but further boluses need dynamic assessment; escalation should be vasopressor rather than reflex fluid (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign).

options.text: Intravenous noradrenaline via peripheral access titrated to a mean arterial pressure at least 65 mmHg
options.rationale: Surviving Sepsis and ANZICS guidance advise starting noradrenaline early alongside fluid resuscitation when MAP remains under 65 mmHg after an initial bolus; peripheral use is acceptable until central access (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign; ANZICS Statement on Peripheral Vasopressors).

options.text: Insulin infusion targeted to blood glucose 4 to 6 mmol/L in the emergency department
options.rationale: Tight glucose control (4 to 6 mmol/L) worsens outcomes in critical illness; target is 6 to 10 mmol/L and it is not part of the hour-1 bundle (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign).

explanation.summary: The sepsis hour-1 bundle asks the clinician to measure lactate, take blood cultures before antibiotics, give broad spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour, start 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate over 4, and start vasopressor if MAP remains under 65 mmHg. Noradrenaline is first line and may be commenced peripherally through a large forearm cannula until central access is placed. Hydrocortisone 200 mg/day is added for refractory shock requiring rising vasopressor. Repeat lactate at 2 to 4 hours to monitor response. In elderly with limited reserve, avoid mandatory fluid overload beyond 30 mL/kg without dynamic assessment.
key_points: Hour-1 bundle: lactate, cultures before antibiotics, antibiotics within 1 hour, 30 mL/kg crystalloid, vasopressor if MAP under 65
Noradrenaline is first line vasopressor
Peripheral noradrenaline is acceptable via large cannula for a limited time
Hydrocortisone for refractory shock only
Target glucose 6 to 10 mmol/L, not 4 to 6
explanation.pearls: The Surviving Sepsis 2021 update endorses initiating vasopressor within the first hour rather than waiting the full 3 hours of fluid, provided the initial fluid response is inadequate; earlier vasopressor is associated with reduced mortality.

subtopic_detail: Adult meningitis empirical antibiotic and adjunctive dexamethasone
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar. A 46 year old previously well woman presents with 12 hours of severe headache, neck stiffness, photophobia and one episode of vomiting. She has no rash. She has no immunosuppression, no recent travel, no contact with meningitis, and no penicillin allergy.

On examination she is drowsy but rousable. Vital signs are pulse 108, blood pressure 132/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 38.6 degrees Celsius. Kernig's sign is positive and she has photophobia. There are no focal neurological signs, no papilloedema and no seizures. Capillary glucose is 5.8 mmol/L (3.5-7.7).

Blood cultures have been drawn, IV access is established, and a CT head has been requested because of the reduced level of consciousness before lumbar puncture. The CT is expected within 30 minutes.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108, BP 132/78 mmHg, RR 20, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 38.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, positive Kernig's sign, photophobia, no focal neurology, no papilloedema
data_table.Investigations: Capillary glucose 5.8 mmol/L (3.5-7.7); CT head requested

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate step?

options.text: Benzylpenicillin 2.4 g intravenous alone as monotherapy for suspected meningococcal disease
options.rationale: Empirical coverage under Therapeutic Guidelines is ceftriaxone rather than benzylpenicillin monotherapy because pneumococcus is the most common adult pathogen and resistant strains exist (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Wait for CT head then perform LP before giving any antibiotic or dexamethasone
options.rationale: Any delay in antibiotic administration in suspected bacterial meningitis worsens outcome; CT and LP can follow the first dose (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Dexamethasone 10 mg intravenous plus ceftriaxone 2 g intravenous without waiting for CT or LP
options.rationale: AU Therapeutic Guidelines advise not delaying antibiotics in suspected bacterial meningitis; ceftriaxone 2 g IV plus dexamethasone 10 mg IV are given before or with LP and dexamethasone must be given before or within 15 minutes of antibiotics for maximum benefit (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Ceftriaxone 2 g intravenous alone with dexamethasone deferred until CSF Gram stain returns
options.rationale: Dexamethasone must be given before or with the first antibiotic dose to blunt the inflammatory response; delaying dexamethasone until CSF returns forfeits mortality benefit in pneumococcal meningitis (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Aciclovir 10 mg/kg intravenous 8 hourly alone for suspected HSV encephalitis
options.rationale: Aciclovir is added when encephalitis features (focal signs, seizures, altered mental state without meningism) are present; her picture is meningitis and needs antibiotic plus steroid (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Bacterial meningitis in adults is a medical emergency. Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis account for the majority; Listeria is a concern in patients over 50, pregnant, or immunosuppressed and adds benzylpenicillin (or add amoxicillin) to ceftriaxone. Dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours for 4 days reduces mortality and neurological sequelae in pneumococcal meningitis when given before or within 15 minutes of the first antibiotic dose. Do not delay antibiotics for CT or LP: draw blood cultures then give the first dose. CT before LP is required for reduced consciousness, focal signs, seizures, immunosuppression, or papilloedema.
key_points: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV plus dexamethasone 10 mg IV without delay
Dexamethasone must be given before or with first antibiotic
Add benzylpenicillin (or amoxicillin) for Listeria over 50
CT before LP if reduced consciousness, focal signs, seizures
Do not delay antibiotic for CT or LP
explanation.pearls: In meningococcal disease dexamethasone gives no mortality benefit but is not withheld empirically because the aetiology is unknown at the bedside; the pneumococcal benefit dominates AU practice.

subtopic_detail: Necrotising soft tissue infection recognition with LRINEC scoring
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar. A 62 year old man with type 2 diabetes presents with 24 hours of increasingly severe pain in his left calf after a minor gardening scratch 3 days ago. His pain is out of proportion to the visible findings and he is now unable to weight bear.

On examination the calf is erythematous with poorly defined borders, warm, and exquisitely tender across an area larger than the visible erythema. There is one small area of dusky discolouration and a haemorrhagic blister. Vital signs are pulse 118, blood pressure 108/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 39.1 degrees Celsius. Investigations: haemoglobin 122 g/L (135-175), white cells 21 x10^9/L (4-11), platelets 168 x10^9/L (150-400), sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 148 micromol/L (60-110), CRP 320 mg/L (under 10), lactate 3.2 mmol/L (under 2), glucose 15.4 mmol/L (3.5-7.7).

He has no penicillin allergy and blood cultures have been drawn. The bedside handheld ultrasound is not diagnostic for gas.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118, BP 108/62 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 39.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Left calf erythema with poorly defined borders, pain out of proportion, dusky discolouration and haemorrhagic blister
data_table.Investigations: Hb 122 g/L (135-175), WCC 21 x10^9/L (4-11), platelets 168 x10^9/L (150-400), Na 132 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 148 micromol/L (60-110), CRP 320 mg/L (<10), lactate 3.2 mmol/L (<2), glucose 15.4 mmol/L (3.5-7.7)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Urgent surgical consult for exploration plus broad spectrum antibiotics
options.rationale: Pain out of proportion, haemorrhagic bullae, systemic toxicity, and high LRINEC score (Hb, WCC, Na, creatinine, CRP, glucose scoring at least 8) mandate urgent surgical debridement rather than imaging or antibiotics alone (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; AU Necrotising Soft Tissue Infection Consensus).
source_refs: AU Necrotising Soft Tissue Infection Consensus

options.text: IV flucloxacillin 2 g 6 hourly and admit under general medicine for 48 hour reassessment
options.rationale: Flucloxacillin monotherapy does not cover the polymicrobial spectrum and delays the definitive surgical intervention that is time critical (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: MRI of the lower limb to confirm fascial involvement before considering surgery
options.rationale: MRI delays surgery in a haemodynamically compromised patient with high clinical suspicion; imaging cannot rule out necrotising infection and clinical judgement drives operation (Source: AU Necrotising Soft Tissue Infection Consensus).
source_refs: AU Necrotising Soft Tissue Infection Consensus

options.text: Hyperbaric oxygen therapy as first line without concurrent surgical exploration
options.rationale: Hyperbaric oxygen is an adjunct after surgical debridement not a substitute; delaying surgery increases mortality (Source: AU Necrotising Soft Tissue Infection Consensus).
source_refs: AU Necrotising Soft Tissue Infection Consensus

options.text: IV immunoglobulin 2 g/kg for suspected streptococcal toxic shock without surgery
options.rationale: IVIG may be adjunctive in streptococcal toxic shock but does not replace source control by surgical debridement (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Necrotising soft tissue infection has a mortality that rises sharply for every hour of delay to source control. Clinical hallmarks are pain out of proportion, systemic toxicity, dusky discolouration, haemorrhagic bullae, and rapid extension. LRINEC uses CRP, WCC, haemoglobin, sodium, creatinine and glucose with a score at least 6 warranting strong suspicion and at least 8 making it highly likely. Empirical antibiotics are broad polymicrobial (piperacillin tazobactam plus vancomycin plus clindamycin for toxin suppression), and the definitive treatment is urgent surgical exploration and debridement.
key_points: Pain out of proportion is the earliest sign
LRINEC at least 6 suspicious, at least 8 highly likely
Empirical polymicrobial cover including clindamycin
Urgent surgical debridement is definitive treatment
Imaging must not delay operation
explanation.pearls: Clindamycin is added even in beta lactam cover because it suppresses streptococcal exotoxin production in the ribosome-bound state, unaffected by the inoculum effect that reduces beta lactam efficacy in high bacterial load.

sources.label: AU Necrotising Soft Tissue Infection Consensus

subtopic_detail: Adrenal crisis in a patient on chronic prednisolone
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar. A 58 year old woman with rheumatoid arthritis on prednisolone 7.5 mg orally daily for 3 years is brought in with 24 hours of vomiting, diarrhoea and lethargy. She was hospitalised 2 days ago for a similar gastroenteritis episode and discharged after clinical improvement, but at that time she was unable to keep her prednisolone down for 48 hours and her general practitioner did not adjust her dose.

On examination she is drowsy and looks unwell. Vital signs are pulse 128, blood pressure 88/52 mmHg lying and unrecordable standing, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees Celsius. She is warm and mildly hyperpigmented in the palmar creases. Bloods: sodium 128 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 5.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), glucose 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-7.7), creatinine 128 micromol/L (45-90), venous pH 7.30 (7.35-7.45), bicarbonate 18 mmol/L (22-32), lactate 2.2 mmol/L (under 2).

Her other medications are methotrexate 15 mg weekly and folic acid, and she has no known adrenal disease.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128, BP 88/52 mmHg lying and unrecordable standing, RR 22, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, unwell, warm, mild palmar crease hyperpigmentation
data_table.Investigations: Na 128 mmol/L (135-145), K 5.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), glucose 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-7.7), creatinine 128 micromol/L (45-90), venous pH 7.30 (7.35-7.45), bicarbonate 18 mmol/L (22-32), lactate 2.2 mmol/L (<2)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Vasopressin infusion at 0.03 units/min to correct hypotension without steroid therapy
options.rationale: Vasopressor without steroid does not address the underlying cortisol deficiency and delays the definitive treatment (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Dexamethasone 8 mg intravenous while awaiting a short synacthen test for definitive diagnosis
options.rationale: Dexamethasone does not interfere with cortisol assay but delays mineralocorticoid effect; hydrocortisone provides both glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid activity and is the AU standard in crisis (Source: Endocrine Society Adrenal Insufficiency Guideline).

options.text: Increase her regular oral prednisolone dose to 15 mg daily and observe for improvement
options.rationale: Oral therapy cannot be absorbed reliably in a vomiting patient with shock and does not deliver the stress dose required in crisis (Source: Endocrine Society Adrenal Insufficiency Guideline).

options.text: Fludrocortisone 200 micrograms intramuscular alone for mineralocorticoid replacement
options.rationale: Fludrocortisone provides mineralocorticoid effect at 3 to 6 hours and is unnecessary while high dose hydrocortisone (which has intrinsic mineralocorticoid activity) is running (Source: Endocrine Society Adrenal Insufficiency Guideline).

options.text: Hydrocortisone 100 mg intravenous bolus and intravenous 0.9 percent sodium chloride resuscitation
options.rationale: Iatrogenic adrenal insufficiency from chronic steroid can precipitate crisis when stress dosing fails during illness; hydrocortisone 100 mg IV plus fluid resuscitation is the immediate treatment before further investigation (Source: Endocrine Society Adrenal Insufficiency Guideline; Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

explanation.summary: Iatrogenic adrenal insufficiency is the most common cause of adrenal crisis in Australia and occurs in patients on the equivalent of prednisolone 5 mg or more for more than 4 weeks. Illness stress dose failure (vomiting, gastroenteritis, sepsis, trauma, surgery) precipitates crisis presenting with hypotension, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia. Immediate management is hydrocortisone 100 mg IV bolus then 200 mg over 24 hours (as infusion or 50 mg 6 hourly) plus 0.9 percent sodium chloride resuscitation and glucose correction. Once stable, taper to twice or thrice usual daily oral dose during illness and educate about sick day rules and injectable emergency kits.
key_points: Steroid over 5 mg prednisolone for 4 weeks risks HPA suppression
Crisis presents with hypotension, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia
Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV bolus then 200 mg over 24 hours
IV fluid and glucose correction alongside steroid
Educate on sick day rules and injectable emergency hydrocortisone
explanation.pearls: The sick day rule taught by Australian endocrine services is to double the usual oral dose for minor illness and triple for major illness; parenteral hydrocortisone 100 mg IM is used if oral cannot be tolerated.

subtopic_detail: Massive transfusion protocol activation and initial component ratio
stem:
You are the trauma team leader in a metropolitan emergency department. A 34 year old man is brought in by ambulance after being struck by a car at high speed. He is on the trauma trolley and reports severe abdominal pain.

He has a distended tender abdomen with pelvic tenderness. Vital signs on arrival are pulse 142, blood pressure 78/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 28, SpO2 96 percent on 15 L/min oxygen non-rebreather, temperature 35.2 degrees Celsius. A rapid FAST scan is positive with free fluid in Morison's pouch and the pouch of Douglas. Blood tests are pending but the initial venous blood gas shows lactate 6.8 mmol/L (under 2), base deficit -12 mmol/L, haemoglobin 82 g/L (135-175). The initial 500 mL crystalloid bolus has produced no improvement in blood pressure. Two 14 gauge intravenous cannulae are in situ and the operating theatre is being prepared for immediate laparotomy.

The consultant surgeon requests the massive transfusion protocol be activated.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 142, BP 78/40 mmHg, RR 28, SpO2 96% on 15 L/min O2, temperature 35.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Distended tender abdomen with pelvic tenderness; positive FAST in Morison's pouch and pouch of Douglas
data_table.Investigations: VBG lactate 6.8 mmol/L (<2), base deficit -12 mmol/L, haemoglobin 82 g/L (135-175); initial 500 mL crystalloid ineffective

lead_in: Which single initial blood component ratio is delivered on massive transfusion activation under Australian trauma guidance?

options.text: Whole blood exclusively as first line without component therapy
options.rationale: Whole blood is not routinely stocked in Australian civilian trauma centres; component therapy in 1:1:1 remains the standard (Source: National Blood Authority Massive Transfusion Guidelines).
source_refs: National Blood Authority Massive Transfusion Guidelines

options.text: Packed red cells and fresh frozen plasma in a 2:1 unit ratio without platelets
options.rationale: PROPPR showed improved 24 hour mortality from haemorrhage with 1:1:1 rather than 2:1:1 ratios; withholding platelets is not AU practice (Source: PROPPR trial; National Blood Authority Massive Transfusion Guidelines).
source_refs: National Blood Authority Massive Transfusion Guidelines

options.text: Packed red cells with cryoprecipitate as first pack without platelets or plasma
options.rationale: Cryoprecipitate is added when fibrinogen falls under 1.5 g/L (or under 2.0 in obstetric haemorrhage) and is not part of the initial 1:1:1 pack (Source: National Blood Authority Massive Transfusion Guidelines).
source_refs: National Blood Authority Massive Transfusion Guidelines

options.text: Packed red cells, fresh frozen plasma and platelets in a 1:1:1 unit ratio
options.rationale: Australian trauma pathways align with PROPPR trial evidence and NBA guidance using 1:1:1 unit ratio (RBC:FFP:platelets) in the first pack of massive transfusion (Source: National Blood Authority Massive Transfusion Guidelines; ANZCA Blood Management).
source_refs: National Blood Authority Massive Transfusion Guidelines

options.text: Packed red cells alone with prothrombin complex concentrate at 25 units/kg
options.rationale: PCC is used for warfarin reversal or specific factor deficiency rather than as first line trauma pack; component ratio is the primary approach (Source: National Blood Authority Massive Transfusion Guidelines).
source_refs: National Blood Authority Massive Transfusion Guidelines

explanation.summary: Massive transfusion in Australia is activated for suspected requirement of at least 5 units of red cells in the first 3 hours, hemorrhagic shock with pending or ongoing bleeding, and validated triggers (Assessment of Blood Consumption score, shock index, base deficit). The National Blood Authority pack delivers red cells, FFP and platelets in a 1:1:1 unit ratio, supported by the PROPPR trial showing lower haemorrhagic death at 24 hours. Add tranexamic acid 1 g IV loading then 1 g over 8 hours if within 3 hours of trauma, and correct hypocalcaemia, acidosis and hypothermia.
key_points: 1:1:1 unit ratio (RBC:FFP:platelets) supported by PROPPR
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 hours of trauma
Cryoprecipitate when fibrinogen under 1.5 g/L
Correct calcium (citrate binds), avoid hypothermia and acidosis
Definitive control is surgical or angiographic
explanation.pearls: Every 4 units of packed red cells contain around 12 mmol of citrate; give 10 mL of 10 percent calcium gluconate IV after every 4 units to prevent hypocalcaemia-induced hypotension and coagulopathy.

sources.label: National Blood Authority Massive Transfusion Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Type B aortic dissection blood pressure and heart rate control
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar. A 68 year old man presents with sudden onset severe tearing back pain radiating between his shoulder blades. He has hypertension on perindopril and amlodipine and smokes 15 cigarettes a day.

On examination he is diaphoretic. Vital signs are pulse 108, blood pressure 208/122 mmHg in the right arm and 188/104 mmHg in the left arm, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 96 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius. Both radial pulses are palpable. Heart sounds are normal without a diastolic murmur, chest is clear, and abdomen is soft. CT aortogram shows an intimal flap originating distal to the left subclavian artery extending to the diaphragm, with no branch vessel involvement, no aortic root involvement, and no pericardial effusion. Troponin I is 15 ng/L (under 34) and creatinine is 88 micromol/L (60-110).

Intravenous access is established and the cardiothoracic surgical team have been contacted; his blood pressure and heart rate must be controlled before transfer.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108, BP 208/122 mmHg right arm and 188/104 mmHg left arm, RR 22, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic, both radial pulses palpable, no diastolic murmur, clear chest, soft abdomen
data_table.CT aortogram: Intimal flap distal to left subclavian, extends to diaphragm, no branch involvement, no aortic root involvement, no pericardial effusion

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate first line pharmacological therapy?

options.text: Intravenous sodium nitroprusside as monotherapy titrated for a systolic target under 120 mmHg
options.rationale: Vasodilator monotherapy causes reflex tachycardia and increases aortic shear stress, worsening dissection propagation; beta blockade first is essential (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Aortic Dissection Position Statement).

options.text: Intravenous esmolol titrated to heart rate 60 beats per minute then intravenous glyceryl trinitrate for blood pressure
options.rationale: Type B dissection is managed initially with impulse control: heart rate 60 to 80 first with a short acting intravenous beta blocker (esmolol titratable), then vasodilator (GTN, sodium nitroprusside) for systolic target under 120 mmHg to reduce shear stress (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Aortic Dissection Position Statement; Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular).

options.text: Intravenous morphine sulfate 5 mg with observation for spontaneous blood pressure improvement
options.rationale: Analgesia is important adjunct but does not achieve haemodynamic targets alone; pharmacological impulse control is required (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular).

options.text: Intravenous hydralazine 10 mg bolus with no additional heart rate control with senior clinical review
options.rationale: Hydralazine causes reflex tachycardia and is contraindicated as first line in dissection; impulse control requires beta blockade before vasodilator (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Aortic Dissection Position Statement).

options.text: Immediate open surgical repair with cardiopulmonary bypass before pharmacological therapy
options.rationale: Type B dissection without branch vessel or organ malperfusion is managed medically first; type A is the surgical emergency (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Aortic Dissection Position Statement).

explanation.summary: Aortic dissection is classified as type A (involves ascending aorta, surgical emergency) or type B (descending only, medical management first with endovascular repair if complicated). Impulse control lowers shear stress driving propagation: heart rate 60 to 80 with intravenous beta blocker (esmolol, labetalol, metoprolol) before or simultaneously with vasodilator (sodium nitroprusside, glyceryl trinitrate) for systolic under 120 mmHg. Vasodilator monotherapy causes reflex tachycardia and worsens shear. Analgesia is essential. Complicated type B (malperfusion, rupture, refractory pain or hypertension) requires TEVAR (thoracic endovascular aortic repair).
key_points: Type A is surgical emergency, type B is medical first
Heart rate control before vasodilator to avoid reflex tachycardia
Target HR 60 to 80, systolic BP under 120 mmHg
Esmolol is titratable IV beta blocker of choice
Complicated type B needs TEVAR
explanation.pearls: Systolic blood pressure difference of at least 20 mmHg between arms in the setting of tearing chest or back pain has a positive likelihood ratio around 5 for dissection; measure both arms in every suspected case.

subtopic_detail: Suspected phaeochromocytoma crisis, alpha blockade before beta blockade
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar. A 44 year old man presents with 3 months of episodic headache, palpitations and sweating and a 24 hour episode of severe headache with palpitations. He has been recently commenced on metoprolol 50 mg twice daily by his general practitioner 3 days ago for suspected hypertension.

On arrival his vital signs are pulse 118, blood pressure 232/136 mmHg, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 37.1 degrees Celsius. His examination is unremarkable apart from diaphoresis and pallor. Urgent bloods show sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), creatinine 108 micromol/L (60-110), troponin I 62 ng/L (under 34), glucose 9.4 mmol/L (3.5-7.7). ECG shows sinus tachycardia with no ST changes. CT chest and abdomen ordered because of the classic triad shows a 5 cm heterogeneous right adrenal mass with washout characteristics suggesting phaeochromocytoma.

His wife has just handed you a fasting fractionated plasma metanephrines result from 2 weeks ago: normetanephrine 8.4 nmol/L (under 1.1) and metanephrine 3.2 nmol/L (under 0.5).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118, BP 232/136 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Na 138 mmol/L (135-145), K 4.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), creatinine 108 micromol/L (60-110), troponin I 62 ng/L (<34), glucose 9.4 mmol/L (3.5-7.7); ECG sinus tachycardia no ST changes; CT 5 cm right adrenal mass with washout characteristics
data_table.Medication: Metoprolol 50 mg twice daily started 3 days ago

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate step in his management?

options.text: Cease metoprolol and commence intravenous phentolamine 2 mg bolus titrated to blood pressure
options.rationale: Unopposed beta blockade in phaeochromocytoma leaves alpha-mediated vasoconstriction to worsen hypertensive crisis; ceasing metoprolol and giving intravenous alpha blockade (phentolamine) reverses the pathophysiology (Source: Endocrine Society Pheochromocytoma Guideline; Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular).

options.text: Increase metoprolol to 100 mg orally twice daily to achieve tighter heart rate control
options.rationale: Increasing unopposed beta blockade worsens alpha mediated vasoconstriction in phaeochromocytoma; alpha blockade must be established first (Source: Endocrine Society Pheochromocytoma Guideline).

options.text: Commence intravenous glyceryl trinitrate infusion titrated for systolic under 140 mmHg without alpha blockade
options.rationale: GTN reduces preload but does not address the catecholamine driven alpha vasoconstriction; suboptimal in crisis (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular).

options.text: Commence oral phenoxybenzamine 10 mg twice daily as sole therapy in the emergency department
options.rationale: Oral phenoxybenzamine is used for preoperative preparation over 7 to 14 days; in acute crisis intravenous phentolamine (or nitroprusside plus alpha blockade) is required (Source: Endocrine Society Pheochromocytoma Guideline).

options.text: Immediate laparoscopic adrenalectomy without pharmacological preparation under close observation
options.rationale: Operating without alpha blockade risks intraoperative catecholamine storm with fatal arrhythmia and hypertension; preoperative preparation over at least 7 days is mandatory (Source: Endocrine Society Pheochromocytoma Guideline).

explanation.summary: Phaeochromocytoma is a catecholamine secreting tumour classically presenting with paroxysms of headache, palpitations, and diaphoresis and elevated fasting fractionated plasma metanephrines. Beta blockade must never precede alpha blockade because unopposed alpha stimulation causes catastrophic vasoconstriction and hypertensive crisis. In crisis, cease any beta blocker and use intravenous phentolamine (short acting alpha antagonist) or sodium nitroprusside. Preoperative preparation uses oral phenoxybenzamine (non selective, long acting) titrated over 7 to 14 days plus liberal salt and fluid intake to restore intravascular volume; beta blockade is added only after alpha blockade is established to control reflex tachycardia. Laparoscopic adrenalectomy is definitive.
key_points: Alpha before beta blockade in phaeochromocytoma
Fasting fractionated plasma metanephrines confirms diagnosis
IV phentolamine or nitroprusside in acute crisis
Preoperative phenoxybenzamine 7 to 14 days plus salt loading
Definitive treatment is laparoscopic adrenalectomy
explanation.pearls: Suspect phaeochromocytoma in patients with the triad of headache, palpitations and diaphoresis plus hypertension (positive likelihood ratio around 6 when all three present); the biochemical test of choice is fasting fractionated plasma metanephrines.

subtopic_detail: Discriminating SIADH from cerebral salt wasting after subarachnoid haemorrhage
stem:
You are the neurology registrar on the acute stroke ward. A 62 year old woman is day 6 following a Fisher grade 3 subarachnoid haemorrhage secured by endovascular coiling of an anterior communicating artery aneurysm. She has been on oral nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours and maintenance intravenous 0.9 percent sodium chloride at 100 mL/h.

Over 24 hours her serum sodium has fallen from 138 to 124 mmol/L (135-145) and she has become confused. Vital signs are pulse 96, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg (baseline 132/78), respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius. Fluid balance shows urine output 4200 mL and intake 2400 mL over the last 24 hours. Bedside examination shows dry mucous membranes and a capillary refill of 3 seconds. Bloods: sodium 124 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.8 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), urea 9.4 mmol/L (3.0-8.0), creatinine 92 micromol/L (45-90), serum osmolality 258 mmol/kg (275-295), urine sodium 88 mmol/L (over 40), urine osmolality 480 mmol/kg (300-900).

Thyroid function and morning cortisol from 2 days ago were within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 108/64 mmHg (baseline 132/78), RR 16, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Confused, dry mucous membranes, capillary refill 3 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Na 124 mmol/L (135-145), K 3.8 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), urea 9.4 mmol/L (3.0-8.0), creatinine 92 micromol/L (45-90), serum osmolality 258 mmol/kg (275-295), urine Na 88 mmol/L (>40), urine osmolality 480 mmol/kg (300-900)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate management step?

options.text: Fluid restrict to 800 mL/day and repeat sodium in 12 hours with senior clinical review
options.rationale: Fluid restriction is the SIADH answer but is dangerous in cerebral salt wasting after SAH because hypovolaemia predisposes to delayed cerebral ischaemia from vasospasm; the pattern here (hypovolaemia, polyuria, rising urea) is CSW not SIADH (Source: Neurocritical Care Society Guideline; Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Commence oral tolvaptan 15 mg once daily as first line therapy for suspected SIADH
options.rationale: Tolvaptan (vasopressin V2 receptor antagonist) treats SIADH but is contraindicated in hypovolaemic hyponatraemia and worsens CSW; the fluid balance and hypotension here point to CSW (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Commence hypertonic 3 percent saline infusion at 30 mL/h with hourly sodium checks
options.rationale: Cerebral salt wasting after SAH is treated with volume replacement and sodium; hypertonic saline restores intravascular volume and sodium simultaneously, corrects the hyponatraemia at a safe rate, and preserves cerebral perfusion (Source: Neurocritical Care Society Guideline; ANZICS SAH Consensus).

options.text: Give demeclocycline 300 mg orally 6 hourly to reduce renal responsiveness to ADH
options.rationale: Demeclocycline treats SIADH by producing nephrogenic diabetes insipidus but is inappropriate for CSW where the pathophysiology is inappropriate natriuresis rather than water retention (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Free water restriction 500 mL/day with intravenous mannitol 20 percent 250 mL over 30 minutes
options.rationale: Mannitol adds osmotic diuresis and worsens hypovolaemia; fluid restriction reduces cerebral perfusion in vasospasm risk period (Source: Neurocritical Care Society Guideline).

explanation.summary: Hyponatraemia after subarachnoid haemorrhage is common and the distinction between SIADH and cerebral salt wasting is critical because their treatments are opposite. SIADH is euvolaemic (or slightly hypervolaemic), with urine osmolality above 100 mmol/kg, urine sodium above 30 mmol/L, and treated with fluid restriction. CSW is hypovolaemic, has high urine output, high urine sodium, rising urea to creatinine ratio, and treated with volume plus sodium replacement (isotonic or hypertonic saline). In SAH, fluid restriction is dangerous because vasospasm and delayed cerebral ischaemia are precipitated by hypovolaemia between days 4 and 14. Correction rate is 8 to 10 mmol/L in 24 hours to avoid osmotic demyelination.
key_points: SIADH is euvolaemic; CSW is hypovolaemic
CSW after SAH is treated with volume plus sodium
Fluid restriction in SAH-related CSW worsens vasospasm risk
Sodium correction 8 to 10 mmol/L per 24 hours
Nimodipine reduces delayed cerebral ischaemia after SAH
explanation.pearls: Rising fractional excretion of urate (FEurate over 12 percent) and elevated BNP have been proposed to help distinguish CSW from SIADH but volume status remains the primary bedside discriminator in Australian practice.
